lines.text: Someone copies your AI model. How do you prove it was yours?
A trained model is just a file of numbers. The copy is identical, and nothing in it says who did the work.
But the work leaves a trail. Training is a long walk downhill, every step making the model a little less wrong.
Proof-of-Learning keeps that trail: snapshots along the way, which a verifier can replay to check the walk really happened.
There's a catch. No computer repeats a long calculation exactly, so the check has to accept close enough. And close enough can be faked.
Our work, SecurePoL, closes that gap with a secret. While the model trains, it also learns planted answers to questions only its owner knows.
Mapmakers used the same trick: a street that doesn't exist, hidden in the map to catch anyone who copies it.
Now a claim needs both: a trail that replays, and a model that knows the secret.
A thief can't name the questions. And scrubbing the secret out changes the model, so it stops matching its own trail.
Hiding that takes real training: the very work they tried to skip.
And the price is small. In our experiments the model stayed almost exactly as accurate, and training took only a little longer.
This matters wherever a model changes hands.
A hospital can confirm its model is the one that was audited.
A carmaker can replay a supplier's training after an incident.
An AI provider can show that a model was trained on licensed data.
AI models are becoming things we buy, deploy and trust. Where a model came from will matter as much as what it can do.
